query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation in multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures under simultaneous wear and corrosion is driven by the mechanical removal of an initially protective oxide film at interphase boundaries, which exposes dissimilar phases that form micro‐galvanic cells. This synergy between oxide film breakdown (via wear) and localized electrochemical dissolution (via galvanic coupling between anodic and cathodic phases) leads to a faster overall degradation rate than would occur from wear or corrosion alone.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a dual-phase microstructure (e.g., combinations of soft and hard phases such as a BCC phase paired with a more noble FCC or ordered intermetallic phase) that, when exposed to high temperatures, forms a thin protective oxide layer along phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Simultaneous exposure to mechanical wear (tribological contact/sliding) and a corrosive environment at an elevated temperature (e.g., 700–900 °C) that challenges the integrity of any passive oxide film.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature corrosive testing (such as in molten salts or aggressive salt solutions) combined with sliding wear actions on the as-formed oxide-protected multi-phase eutectic structure; comparison must be made against conditions where only wear or only corrosion is applied.
generation.structural_mediator: Interphase (or phase boundary) regions where different phases (with distinct electrochemical potentials) abut, and where the oxide film is most readily disrupted by wear, forming local sites for micro-galvanic coupling.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures the alloy’s surface develops a protective oxide film. However, mechanical wear during sliding removes or damages this film, particularly along vulnerable interphase boundaries where dissimilar phases are joined. The exposed phases—with differing tendencies toward oxidation—form micro-galvanic cells that locally accelerate corrosion. This repetitive cycle of oxide film removal and rapid localized dissolution leads to an overall degradation rate that is higher than the sum of isolated wear or corrosion processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear and corrosion, the alloy will exhibit significantly greater mass loss and deeper localized corrosion pits at phase boundaries compared to tests under isolated wear or corrosion. The deterioration will be especially pronounced at regions where the protective oxide is repeatedly disrupted, and the spatial distribution of corrosion will correlate with the micro-galvanic contrasts of adjacent phases.
generation.baseline: The same alloy exposed to either wear only (mechanical sliding under inert, non-corrosive conditions) or corrosion only (static exposure to the corrosive medium without mechanical disruption) at the same temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to prevail when: (a) a protective oxide film forms initially at elevated temperatures, (b) the alloy has an inherently heterogeneous microstructure with phases having sufficiently different electrochemical potentials, and (c) the rate of mechanical wear is high enough to continuously disrupt the passive film. At lower temperatures or in more chemically homogeneous alloys, this coupled effect should be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain what the precise quantitative contribution of the oxide film loss versus the intrinsic micro-galvanic coupling is. Additionally, the degree to which alloy-specific parameters (e.g., oxide composition, phase distribution, and intrinsic electrochemical potentials) influence the overall degradation rate is not yet fully defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the eutectic high-entropy alloy and subject them to three separate treatments at an elevated temperature: (a) solely mechanical wear (in a non-corrosive inert atmosphere), (b) solely corrosion (static exposure in the corrosive medium without mechanical action), and (c) simultaneous wear–corrosion. Use identical sliding wear parameters (load, speed) and maintain the corrosive environment (e.g., aggressive salt solution or molten salt). Use surface-sensitive techniques to image oxide film integrity and map local electrochemical potentials at phase boundaries.
measurements: Total mass loss and pit depth measurements via profilometry or gravimetric analysis
High-resolution electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess oxide film continuity and phase boundary integrity
Local electrochemical measurements (e.g., scanning Kelvin probe force microscopy) to detect micro-galvanic areas
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to quantify passive film breakdown and charge transfer resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simultaneous wear–corrosion condition does not produce a significantly higher total degradation (mass loss, pit depth, and localized corrosion activity at phase boundaries) than the sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only conditions, or if no localized micro-galvanic activity is detected at interphase boundaries, then the hypothesis that oxide film breakdown coupled with micro-galvanic corrosion is responsible for the accelerated degradation will be falsified.

Question: Do high-entropy nanoalloys exhibit the theoretically predicted sluggish diffusion and enhanced thermal stability, or do they undergo phase separation and structural evolution at high temperatures?. System: AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy nanoalloys (HENA), specifically near-equimolar compositions (≈Au20Co28Cu11Ni20Pt21) with diameters of 3–6.5 nm.. Processing: Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) on amorphous 50 nm SiN membranes or 5 nm carbon films; substrate temperature 873 K, laser frequency 5 Hz, total nominal thickness 4 nm.. Test conditions: In situ aberration-corrected STEM heating from 298 to 973 K (steps at 473, 673, 773, 873, 973 K) with a heating rate of 1 K s⁻¹; MD simulations from 400 to 1500 K using EAM potentials.. Findings: Particle size distribution remains unchanged at 473 K but widens up to 13 nm at 973 K due to coalescence of smallest NPs (2–4 nm).; NPs reshape from elliptical to spherical shapes as the in-plane shape ratio increases with temperature.; Phase separation occurs progressively with temperature, driven by the segregation of Au and Cu to the NP surface.; At 973 K, a complete loss of gold and copper is observed due to the melting and evaporation
